title: The Book Named for His Wife
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: a story people tell about a scholar who wrote careful books on schools that disagreed, and named one of them after his wife
carry: one truth, six darshanas: lenses, not team jerseys
tomorrow: Krishna is leaving, and his friend asks to come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two garlands, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and brahmarpanam: every act, even a meal, offered to Brahman.

There's a story people tell about a scholar named Vachaspati Mishra. He was writing a commentary, and he worked at it so long and so completely that he lost track of everything else, including the woman who kept the lamp lit beside him, his wife. When he finally looked up and asked who she was, she told him. Moved, so the story goes, he named the book after her: the Bhamati. The story may be legend. But the scholar's shelf is real, and it's strange. On the last day of this part, it shows how to hold all six darshanas at once.
screen: `A SCHOLAR BENT OVER HIS BOOK.` → `THE ONE WHO KEPT THE LAMP LIT.` → `A BOOK NAMED FOR HER.`

segments.voice: Here's what's strange about the shelf. The Bhamati is a Vedanta commentary, in Shankara's line. But Vachaspati Mishra is also remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, on Samkhya, on Yoga and on Mimamsa. Schools that argue with each other, sometimes sharply. Among them, a commentary on a book by Mandana Mishra, yesterday's debater. And he wrote on each of them from the inside, carefully, laying out its case in its own terms. That's what a lens is. Not a team jersey. A way of seeing you learn well enough to look through. So here are all six, one last time. Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching? Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on? Why can one tradition hold all six? Many Hindus reach for a line from the Rig Veda: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. It's about the names of the divine, but many teachers read it as the spirit of the six schools too. That's the teaching to keep: in Hinduism, a darshana is a way of seeing, and one truth can be seen from more than one side. It ends with no winner. That's the point of the part we're closing, schools of thought, never ranked. The tradition kept all six on one shelf, argued among them for a long time, and kept the lamp lit for the next reader. Tomorrow the lineage track picks up again, with a different teacher, Krishna speaking to his friend Uddhava in the Bhagavata, on action.
screen: `ONE SCHOLAR, MANY SCHOOLS.` · `A LENS, NOT A TEAM JERSEY.` · `TRUTH IS ONE; MANY NAMES.` · `SIX WAYS OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Picture the first ordinary thing you'll do tomorrow morning, filling a kettle, finding your keys, opening a door, and let whichever of the six questions arrives first stand in front of it. Look through it for a few breaths and notice what comes into focus, then set the lens down and rest in the plain scene without any question at all. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.
Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, each tried for a day, none of them ranked. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one truth, six darshanas, lenses, not team jerseys. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1201 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KRISHNA IS LEAVING. TAKE ME WITH YOU.`

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of Vachaspati Mishra's Vedanta commentary, which a story ties to his wife.

trapdoor: what you thought: each Hindu scholar belonged to one school and attacked the others.
what it means: a scholar could learn each darshana from the inside and set out its case fairly, as a lens rather than a team, in the spirit of 'truth is one, the wise call it by many names'.
what a scholar hears: Vachaspati Mishra's commentaries across the darshanas, including the Bhamati on Shankara's Brahma Sutra Bhashya, the Tattva-kaumudi on Samkhya and the Tattva-vaisharadi on Yoga.

chat.says: Sam's been reading up 📚 'wait, hindus have SIX philosophies that argue with each other?? how is that one religion' 😅
options: they kept all six on one shelf. one scholar wrote on almost all of them from the inside. truth is one, the wise call it by many names.

chat.meaning: Vachaspati Mishra wrote careful commentaries on schools that argue with each other; many Hindus hold the six as ways of seeing one truth, in the spirit of the Rig Veda's 'truth is one, the wise call it by many names'.

notes: The Bhamati naming story is traditional legend; the script says so twice. Confirm the telling (details vary).

Vachaspati Mishra's commentaries: Bhamati (Advaita), Tattva-kaumudi (Samkhya), Tattva-vaisharadi (Yoga), Nyaya-vartika-tatparya-tika (Nyaya), Nyaya-kanika and Tattva-bindu (Mimamsa). No Vaisheshika commentary is claimed. Confirm.
